clue.text: Penny once one to stick on her side

definitions.note: a cryptic pointer to the phrase 'distaff side', the female line of a family; the answer alone is the spinning rod

blocks.note: D was the symbol for the old pre-decimal British penny
the Roman numeral
a staff is a stout stick

explanation.surface: A girl called Penny, long ago, being one to stick up for her own side.
explanation.walkthrough: Penny looks like a girl's name; 'once' marks the old penny, abbreviated D before 1971 decimalisation. Her side is the distaff side, the mother's side of a family.
explanation.definitionFit: A distaff is the rod used in hand spinning, a traditionally female task, so the phrase names maternal relatives.

clue.text: Outwit the clergy - this should make them dry up!

definitions.text: this should make them dry up!
definitions.note: a cryptic description of the thing; 'them' is the dishes

blocks.note: to dish someone is to defeat or frustrate them
the cloth is a collective name for clergymen

explanation.surface: A trick to silence talkative priests.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dry up' suggests making the clergy stop talking; the answer dries dishes.
explanation.definitionFit: A tea towel is used for wiping washed crockery until it is no longer wet.

clue.text: They may practise curing - or need it?

blocks.note: first meaning: people who preserve fish or meat over wood fires
second meaning: people addicted to tobacco who could use a cure for the habit

explanation.surface: Doctors who practise medicine, or patients who need it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Curing' suggests medicine; the first sense is preserving fish or ham with smoke.
explanation.definitionFit: Kippers and bacon are cured by people who smoke them, while tobacco users might wish to be cured of it.

clue.text: Constituents of Cheam put a Tory in - farmer's wife perhaps

indicators.note: constituents are component parts, so the letters lie within the following words

blocks.note: running across the four words

explanation.surface: Voters of Cheam electing a Conservative MP, with a rural wife looking on.
explanation.walkthrough: Cheam is a suburb of south London. In the nursery rhyme Three Blind Mice, the farmer's wife cuts off their tails with a carving knife.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who severs limbs or tails is an amputator, as the farmer's wife did to the three mice.

clue.text: The lot of a well-fed egghead

blocks.note: plump from eating plenty
read as the head of the word egg, its opening letter

explanation.surface: The life of a plump intellectual.
explanation.walkthrough: Egghead looks like one word for a highbrow, but splits into egg and its head.
explanation.definitionFit: One's lot in life is one's destiny, whatever fortune has allotted to a person.

clue.text: It could be Ginger, or part of his Army bed

blocks.note: first meaning: a ginger nut is a kind of small sweet baked cookie
second meaning: soldiers once slept on three square stuffed mattress sections, each called by this name

explanation.surface: A soldier nicknamed Ginger and the bedding in his barracks.
explanation.walkthrough: Ginger looks like a red-haired soldier's nickname; it is the flavour of a cookie. In British army slang the square mattress pads were 'biscuits'.
explanation.definitionFit: Ginger nuts are a familiar British cookie, and the square pads making up an old army mattress shared the same name.

clue.text: Rickety vehicle - or performer in a Danse Macabre?

blocks.note: first meaning: an old bicycle with solid tyres, or any jolting old car
second meaning: a skeleton dancing in the medieval dance of death rattles its frame

explanation.surface: A shaky old car, or a dancer in Saint-Saëns's spooky piece.
explanation.walkthrough: The Danse Macabre shows skeletons dancing, so a dancer there literally rattles its skeleton.
explanation.definitionFit: Early bicycles jarred riders badly and got this nickname; a dancing skeleton would rattle in the same way.

clue.text: One's personal steamer

blocks.note: surface reading: a private steamship, or a kitchen gadget for cooking vegetables
setter's reading: something that steams a person, a hot room for sweating

explanation.surface: A private steamboat for one's own use.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Steamer' wants to be a boat; it is a room that steams the person inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: A Finnish bathhouse heated with hot stones makes the bather sweat in dry or damp heat.

clue.text: Immature, but prepared to support the United Nations

indicators.note: in a down entry, supporting means sitting underneath, so this piece comes second

blocks.note: the usual abbreviation
set to go

explanation.surface: A young country, inexperienced but willing to back the UN.
explanation.walkthrough: Prepared looks like the opposite of the answer, which makes the surface nicely paradoxical.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone not yet fully developed or fit for a task is not ready for it, so lacks maturity.

clue.text: -Father's so-called herb

indicators.note: so-called means named that way when spoken, signalling a matching sound

blocks.note: Father Time is the old man with a scythe and hourglass

explanation.surface: The garden plant that belongs to Dad.
explanation.walkthrough: The leading dash continues 16 Down: Father Time goes round and round the clock.
explanation.definitionFit: Thyme is a low aromatic garden plant used in cooking, so it is a herb.

clue.text: Exclusive shovel

blocks.note: first meaning: a news story one paper has before its rivals
second meaning: a deep ladle or small spade for lifting loose material

explanation.definitionFit: A newspaper's exclusive story is a scoop, and a scoop is also a short-handled shovel or ladle for loose stuff.

clue.text: He had a second Missus

blocks.note: surface reading: some man who married twice
setter's reading: the title of a Pinero play about a man's second wife, whose surname is the answer

explanation.surface: A remarried husband, described plainly.
explanation.walkthrough: The Second Mrs Tanqueray (1893) is Arthur Wing Pinero's famous play; her husband Aubrey Tanqueray is the 'he' who married again.
explanation.definitionFit: Aubrey Tanqueray in Pinero's drama takes Paula as his second wife, so the play's title names him.

clue.text: Newcastle wedges

blocks.note: split as new plus castle: the six letters of castle, made new by rearrangement

explanation.surface: Wedge-shaped items from the Tyneside city of Newcastle.
explanation.walkthrough: Newcastle reads as one place name; split it into 'New' and 'castle'.
explanation.definitionFit: Cleats are small wedge-shaped blocks fixed to hold ropes in place or to give shoes grip.

clue.text: Flow in Eden endlessly, breaking loose from restraint

definitions.note: a gerund phrase used as a noun, matching the noun answer

indicators.note: without an end means the final letter of the word is cut away
placed in means one piece sits inside the other

blocks.note: taken as written, the biblical garden
Scapa Flow is the naval anchorage in Orkney, so the flow suggests its first word

explanation.surface: A stream in the Garden of Eden that never ends bursting its banks.
explanation.walkthrough: Flow looks like a verb about water; it is the second half of Scapa Flow, the Royal Navy's Orkney anchorage. EDE wrapped round SCAPA gives ESCAPADE.
explanation.definitionFit: An escapade is a reckless adventure in which someone throws off the usual rules and constraints for a while.

clue.text: Outlet intended, we hear, help time-keeping

definitions.note: a noun phrase: a help to time-keeping

indicators.note: we hear means the word is judged by sound when spoken

blocks.note: a way out, as for steam
intended is meant, spelt here as a sound

explanation.surface: An exit, it is said, designed to help with punctuality.
explanation.definitionFit: In a clock or watch the mechanism that releases the gears tick by tick regulates the timekeeping.

clue.text: Ready to be shot in attack

blocks.note: first meaning: an actor waiting at the film studio for filming, split as two words
second meaning: a fierce assault or the beginning of an illness

explanation.surface: A soldier primed for being fired upon during an assault.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Shot' suggests gunfire, but it means filmed: an actor is 'on set' when ready for the camera.
explanation.definitionFit: An onset is an assault or charge, as in the onset of the enemy, and also the start of something.

clue.text: Well equipped to look daggers?

blocks.note: surface reading: good at glaring angrily at someone
setter's reading: daggers are sharp, so one whose gaze is keen and pointed is ideal for it

explanation.surface: Someone with a talent for furious glares.
explanation.walkthrough: To 'look daggers' is to glare; taking daggers literally as sharp things gives the observant answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Being keen-sighted means noticing small details, and the image of pointed blades fits the angry glare idiom.

clue.text: Go round and round the point -

definitions.text: Go round and round the point

blocks.clueFragment: Go round and round the point
blocks.note: surface reading: talk in circles without getting to the matter
setter's reading: a ballet dancer spinning on the tip of the toe

explanation.surface: Someone talking evasively, circling the issue.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The point' suggests an argument; it is the dancer's tip-toe position.
explanation.definitionFit: A full spin on one foot, usually on the toes, is the classic ballet turn.

clue.text: Instrument carrier had so drab an arrangement

indicators.note: an arrangement means the preceding letters are set out in another order

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: An orchestra's instrument van with a dull layout.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Instrument' suggests music; here it means gauges such as a speedometer.
explanation.definitionFit: A car's panel facing the driver holds the dials and gauges, so it bears the instruments.

clue.text: Breathe in, when distressed, and take a long sleep

indicators.note: something distressed is upset and disordered, so the preceding letters are jumbled

blocks.note: taken as written, nine letters

explanation.surface: Advice for coping with stress: deep breathing, then a good long rest.
explanation.definitionFit: Animals that hibernate pass the winter in a dormant state, which is a very extended slumber.

clue.text: Shield that may crumple?

blocks.note: first meaning: a small round shield held by a handle
second meaning: read as a thing that buckles, a whimsical agent noun

explanation.surface: A shield that may collapse under blows.
explanation.definitionFit: A buckler is a small hand-held round shield, and something that buckles gives way or folds under pressure.

clue.text: Optical illusions off the motorway cause storms

indicators.note: off means taken away, so one piece is stripped out of the other

blocks.note: visions of water seen in the desert heat
the M1 is Britain's first motorway, written in crosswords as MI

explanation.surface: Shimmering visions seen beside the highway causing weather trouble.
explanation.walkthrough: The M1, London to Leeds, is read as the letters MI. Remove them from the front of MIRAGES to leave RAGES.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who rages shouts and blusters with fury, just as a person who storms about does.

clue.text: Cheese right for guy to eat before finishing

indicators.note: eating takes something inside, so one piece goes within another
finishing places the next piece at the end of the answer

blocks.note: a fellow
the usual abbreviation
an old word for before

explanation.surface: A recipe: choose the right cheese for a man to eat before he finishes his meal.
explanation.walkthrough: G(R)UY, then ERE: the guy 'eats' R, and ERE ends it.
explanation.definitionFit: Gruyère is a hard Swiss cheese from the district of the same name, a well-known type.

clue.text: Make out a prescription, perhaps, to solve the cryptic?

blocks.note: first meaning: read a doctor's notoriously illegible handwriting
second meaning: crack a coded or puzzling message

explanation.surface: A pharmacist puzzling over a doctor's scrawl.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Make out a prescription' looks like the doctor writing one; here it means managing to read one.
explanation.definitionFit: To decode a cipher or struggle through bad writing is to work out its meaning, which suits both halves.

clue.text: Like St Paul's, none the less condemned

definitions.note: an adjective phrase, matching the adjective answer

indicators.note: less means minus, so one piece is subtracted from the other

blocks.note: nothing, zero
sentenced to a dire fate

explanation.surface: A cathedral that is nonetheless doomed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'None the less' reads as nevertheless, but splits into none (O) and 'the less', minus. DOOMED minus one O.
explanation.definitionFit: Wren's cathedral in London is famous for its great cupola, so it is a rounded-roofed building.

clue.text: Formal in front of a first lady

definitions.note: prima is the Italian feminine form of first

indicators.note: in front of places the first piece ahead of the next

blocks.note: stiffly proper
taken as written

explanation.surface: Stiffly correct before a President's wife.
explanation.walkthrough: First lady suggests a President's wife; it is the literal sense of prima, as in prima donna.
explanation.definitionFit: In Italian prima is the feminine word for first, as in prima donna, the leading female singer.

clue.text: Whither bus without difficulty returns city workers

definitions.note: with 'city workers' it means where commuters return to

indicators.note: without in the old sense of outside, so one word wraps round the other
returning means going back, so the combined letters are read from right to left

blocks.note: taken as written
as in Hamlet's 'there's the rub', a snag

explanation.surface: Asking where a bus that avoids trouble takes office staff home.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Without' is the old sense of outside. The definition is split round the wordplay: whither city workers return, and 'returns' does double duty.
explanation.definitionFit: Commuters leave the city centre at day's end for outlying residential districts, so that is where they head.

clue.text: Get round this to show astonishment

definitions.text: Get round this to show astonishment

blocks.clueFragment: Get round this to show astonishment
blocks.note: surface reading: overcome or evade something to look amazed
setter's reading: place the word round before the answer to make a phrase for wide-open, wondering eyes

explanation.surface: Circumvent this to act surprised.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Get round' suggests circumvent; read literally, put 'round' with the answer: round-eyed, staring in wonder.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone staring in amazement has wide, circular eyes, so the compound describes visible astonishment.

clue.text: Many indisposed to take fashionable Eastern-line hats

blocks.note: M is the Roman numeral for a thousand, a large number
unwell
in fashion
the abbreviation for east
RY is the abbreviation for railway, a line

explanation.surface: Lots of sick people wearing stylish oriental headgear.
explanation.definitionFit: Millinery is the trade in women's headwear, and the collective word for the hats themselves.

clue.text: The bread-and-butter letter

blocks.note: taken as written
a bread-and-butter letter is a note of thanks after a visit, and ta is British slang for thanks

explanation.surface: The polite note a guest sends a host after staying.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bread-and-butter letter' reads as one phrase; it splits into 'thanks' (TA) and the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Theta is the eighth character of the Greek alphabet, so it is a letter in the alphabetic sense.

clue.text: Staying asleep? Don't around Sandhurst!

indicators.note: placed around means the first word surrounds the following one

blocks.note: taken as written, the apostrophe dropped
Sandhurst is the Royal Military Academy, the British army's officer school

explanation.surface: A warning against dozing off near the officer training college.
explanation.definitionFit: Something dormant is inactive as if sleeping, like a volcano or seed lying quietly and waiting.

clue.text: The average person can't stand going in here

definitions.text: The average person can't stand going in here

blocks.clueFragment: The average person can't stand going in here
blocks.note: surface reading: a place most people dislike entering
setter's reading: the water in part of a swimming pool is too high for anyone of ordinary height to touch the bottom

explanation.surface: A spot the ordinary person loathes visiting.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Can't stand' reads as dislike; literally it means being unable to stand on the pool floor.
explanation.definitionFit: The deep part of a swimming pool is where water rises over the head of someone of normal height.
